title: Mobile Man Sentenced to More Than Five Years in Prison for a Cocaine and Crack Cocaine-Trafficking Conspiracy
text:
Mobile Man Sentenced to More Than Five Years in Prison for a Cocaine and Crack Cocaine-Trafficking Conspiracy
Press Release Mobile Man Sentenced to More Than Five Years in Prison for a Cocaine and Crack Cocaine-Trafficking Conspiracy Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Alabama MOBILE, AL – A Mobile man was sentenced to 63 months in federal prison for participating in a conspiracy to traffic cocaine and crack cocaine. According to court documents, Rodney Antwaine Davis, 42, was arrested on November 9, 2023, after leading police officers on a high-speed chase through a residential neighborhood in Mobile. Davis crashed into a ditch and attempted to flee on foot but was apprehended by officers. During the arrest, officers seized $6,145 in cash and a plastic bag containing crack cocaine from Davis’s underwear. A chemist confirmed that the crack cocaine weighed 52.69 grams. On March 20, 2025, federal agents obtained a warrant to search a package mailed from Houston, Texas, to an address on Johnston Street in Mobile under a fictitious name. The package contained more than two kilograms of vacuum-sealed powder cocaine and a bottle containing 300 alprazolam pills, as confirmed by laboratory testing. The following day, an undercover agent delivered the package to the residence on Johnston Street. Davis arrived and retrieved the package. Agents moved in to arrest him, but Davis fled into the house before being apprehended in a bedroom. At the time of his arrest, Davis had $5,734 in cash in his pocket. Agents also discovered a small amount of methamphetamine on a bed near where Davis was arrested and three bottles of promethazine syrup in Davis’s car, which was parked outside the residence. Agents seized and searched Davis’s cell phone, which contained messages and other data related to his drug-trafficking conspiracy. U.S. District Judge Kristi K. DuBose sentenced Davis to a total of 63 months in prison, with his sentence adjusted to account for the 19 months he has spent in custody since March 2025. Upon his release from prison, Davis will serve four years of supervised release, during which he will be subject to drug testing. The ordered Davis to pay $100 in special assessments. U.S. Attorney Sean P. Costello of the Southern District of Alabama made the announcement. Homeland Security Investigations, the United States Postal Inspection Service, the Mobile Police Department, and the Mobile County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Justin Roller prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States. Updated October 16, 2026 Component USAO - Alabama, Southern

title: Shiprock Man Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison for Second-Degree Murder
text:
Shiprock Man Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison for Second-Degree Murder
Press Release Shiprock Man Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison for Second-Degree Murder Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico ALBUQUERQUE – A Shiprock man was sentenced to 20 years in prison for fatally stabbing a man in broad daylight near a community grocery store in Shiprock, New Mexico. According to publicly available court documents, on the afternoon of July 25, 2024, officers with the Navajo Nation Police Department responded to a fight in progress near a high-traffic Navajo Nation shopping center in Shiprock, New Mexico. Upon arrival, they found a man lying on the ground with wounds to his face and chest. Witnesses reported that Edison Brady , 57, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, had stabbed the man in the chest after the man was already badly beaten, hardly conscious, lying on the ground, and bleeding from the head. According to multiple witnesses, Brady attacked the victim without provocation, repeatedly punching and kicking him as he remained on the ground and attempted to shield his face. Brady then walked away, retrieved a long kitchen knife from his nearby bag, and returned to stab the victim in the chest as the victim lay bleeding and barely conscious. The victim died from his injuries shortly after arriving at the Northern Navajo Medical Center. Officers recovered the knife, which was covered in the victim’s blood, from Brady ’s bag minutes after the attack. Brady pleaded guilty without a plea agreement to an indictment charging him with one count of second-degree murder. Upon his release from prison, Brady will be subject to five years of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Brady must also compensate the New Mexico Crime Victim Reparations Commission for the $6,000.00 it expended paying for the victim’s funeral expenses. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today. The Farmington Resident Agency of the FBI’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from Navajo Nation Police Department and Navajo Nation Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant United States Attorneys Jena Ritchey and Zachary C. Jones are prosecuting this case. Press Release Philadelphia Man Convicted for his Role in a $2 Million Theft Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Jersey CAMDEN, N.J. – A Philadelphia man was convicted on October 15, 2026, for his role in stealing $2 million from a Glassboro business and laundering the proceeds of his theft, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced. Ruben Cruz, 33, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and Davenport, Florida, was convicted of one count of conspiracy to transport stolen property across state lines, one count of interstate transportation of stolen property, one count of conspiracy to launder money, and seven counts of money laundering.  Cruz was convicted following a three-day trial before U.S. District Judge Christine P. O’Hearn in Camden federal court.  Sentencing is set for February 24, 2027. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial: Over the 2021 July 4 th holiday weekend, Cruz and co-conspirator Ricky Rivas-Ortiz burglarized a Glassboro business, stealing a safe that contained more than $2 million in money orders and cash and taking it to Philadelphia.  After the burglary, Cruz and another co-conspirator negotiated money orders from the stolen safe in a manner designed to conceal that they were stolen.  One method they used to launder the proceeds was altering the stolen money orders and depositing them in piecemeal fashion.  For example, Cruz deposited some of the stolen money orders on the same day at different banks that were next door to each other and deposited other stolen money orders at the same bank branch over several consecutive days. Rivas-Ortiz previously pleaded guilty to an information charging him with transporting stolen property interstate and was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Christine P. O’Hearn to 21 months’ imprisonment. For Cruz, the count of conspiracy to transport stolen property interstate carries a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000, or twice the gross loss to the victim or gain to the defendant, whichever is greatest.  The count of interstate transportation of stolen property carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000, or twice the gross loss to the victim or gain to the defendant, whichever is greatest.  The count of conspiracy to launder money and each money laundering count carry a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $500,000, or twice the value of the laundered money, whichever is greatest. title: U.S Departments of Justice and Labor Secure Settlement with Cloudera, Enforce Two-Year PERM Debarment & Back Pay Following Discrimination Against U.S. Workers
text:
U.S Departments of Justice and Labor Secure Settlement with Cloudera, Enforce Two-Year PERM Debarment & Back Pay Following Discrimination Against U.S. Workers
Press Release U.S Departments of Justice and Labor Secure Settlement with Cloudera, Enforce Two-Year PERM Debarment & Back Pay Following Discrimination Against U.S. Workers Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs The U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division (CRT) and the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) today announced a coordinated enforcement resolution with Cloudera Inc., a Santa Clara, California-based data management company, following allegations that the company discriminated against qualified U.S. workers during recruitment conducted under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program. “There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against U.S. workers,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This substantial settlement, in partnership with DOL, sends a strong signal to employers that the federal government will work together to ensure employers treat U.S. workers fairly.” As part of the resolution, Cloudera will be barred from participating in the PERM program for two years, one of the most significant sanctions available for DOL to protect the integrity of the employment-based immigration system and safeguard opportunities for U.S. workers. The debarment follows DOL’s earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing and reflects DOL’s commitment to aggressively enforcing labor certification requirements when employers fail to provide U.S. workers a fair opportunity to compete for jobs. The settlement also resolves a lawsuit DOJ filed in April of this year, alleging that Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) by discriminating against U.S. workers when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process. Under the terms of the settlement with the Justice Department, Cloudera will establish a back-pay fund of $1.4 million to compensate qualified U.S. workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Cloudera also will pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States. In addition to the two-year debarment, Cloudera will be subject to compliance obligations designed to ensure future adherence to federal labor and anti-discrimination laws. These measures include enhanced monitoring, revised PERM compliance procedures, and reporting requirements intended to prevent future violations. This debarment and compliance framework establish an important enforcement precedent and strengthen future efforts to protect U.S. workers. Press Release The District of Alaska Joins DOJ Fraud Division, IRS, and IRS-CI in National Tax Enforcement Surge Exposing Over $490 Million in Tax Fraud Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Alaska ANCHORAGE, Alaska – A federal grand jury in Alaska returned an indictment charging a doctor with five counts of attempting to evade and defeat taxes. According to court documents, between January 2018 and May 2024, John Michael Koller, 66, of Kodiak, Alaska, willfully attempted to evade and defeat income tax owed to the United States. During this time, Dr. Koller was the owner and manager of Kodiak Island Ambulatory Care Clinic (KIACC). The indictment alleges that in attempting to evade taxes, Dr. Koller submitted fraudulent corporate and individual income tax returns to the IRS, maintained falsified accounting records, provided tax preparers with incomplete and inaccurate financial information, and made false statements to investigators. Dr. Koller also concealed cash income generated by KIACC by directing employees to record the cash income in separate places, destroying cash receipts and cash deposit slips, and not depositing cash income into bank accounts. Dr. Koller’s initial appearance was held on October 9, 2026, before U.S. Magistrate Judge Kyle F. Reardon of the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman of the District of Alaska; and Special Agent in Charge Adam Jobes of the IRS Criminal Investigation, Seattle Field Office made the announcement. The IRS Criminal Investigation, Seattle Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ainsley McNerney is prosecuting the case. title: Two Plead Guilty to Unemployment Insurance Benefits Fraud Conspiracy
text:
Two Plead Guilty to Unemployment Insurance Benefits Fraud Conspiracy
Press Release Two Plead Guilty to Unemployment Insurance Benefits Fraud Conspiracy Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of California SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Las Vegas residents Ricky Lee Ware, 43, and Kimberly Ann Wallace, 30, pleaded guilty today to conspiracy to commit access device fraud, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced. According to court documents, between July 2020 and January 2021, the defendants conspired to obtain debit cards that allowed them to access unemployment benefits. The unemployment benefits were in the names of people who did not know the defendants. The defendants then used the debit cards to withdraw more than $900,000 in unemployment benefits from ATMs. The U.S. Department of Labor Office of Inspector General, Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation; and the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicholas M. Fogg is prosecuting the case. Ware and Wallace are scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge Dena Coggins on Feb. 19, 2027, and face a maximum of 7.5 years in prison. The actual sentence, however, will be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables. The third defendant in the case, Carlos Lee Sanchez Jr., 46, of Sacramento, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit access device fraud in June 2026 and is scheduled to be sentenced Nov. 13, 2026. This effort is part of a California COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Strike Force operation, one of five interagency COVID-19 fraud strike force teams established by the U.S. Department of Justice. The California Strike Force combines law enforcement and prosecutorial resources in the Eastern and Central Districts of California and focuses on large-scale, multistate pandemic relief fraud perpetrated by criminal organizations and transnational actors. The strike forces use prosecutor-led and data analyst-driven teams to identify and bring to justice those who stole pandemic relief funds. title: D.C. Mother Pleads Guilty to Perjury for Lying to Grand Jury During Investigation into Her 2-Year-Old Son’s Murder
text:
D.C. Mother Pleads Guilty to Perjury for Lying to Grand Jury During Investigation into Her 2-Year-Old Son’s Murder
Press Release D.C. Mother Pleads Guilty to Perjury for Lying to Grand Jury During Investigation into Her 2-Year-Old Son’s Murder Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia USADC.Media@usdoj.gov WASHINGTON – Monet Jones, 28, of Washington, D.C., pleaded guilty today for lying to the grand jury about the beating death of her 2-year-old child, Mars Jones, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. “Two-year-old Mars deserved a mother who would fight for justice, not protect the man who beat her child to death,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Instead, she misled investigators and deleted evidence to shield him from accountability. If you obstruct justice to protect someone who kills a child, you will answer for it. No exceptions.” Jones pleaded guilty before D.C. Superior Court Judge Rainey Brandt to one count of perjury and one count of tampering with evidence. Judge Park scheduled sentencing for February 1, 2027, with her co-defendant, Dasean Matthews. According to the government’s evidence, on October 13, 2022, 2-year-old Mars, Jones, and Matthews, (co-defendant Jones’s romantic partner) drove to a Dunkin Donuts just before noon. While in the Dunkin Donuts, video evidence shows Matthews striking the young child with a closed fist in the upper body causing Mars to fall and slam against a metal railing. Later that day, while in a parking garage, video evidence shows Matthews grabbing Mars by the neck of his clothing, swing him by the clothing, and minutes later, strike Mars in the upper body or face, causing the young child to again fall to the floor. Later the same day, while alone in a vehicle with Mars, video evidence shows defendant Matthews repeatedly strike the young child so forcefully that the vehicle shakes from the impact of the blows. Immediately thereafter, Matthews delivers an unconscious and bloody baby Mars to Jones and then flees the scene. An autopsy determined that Mars died from complications of inflicted head trauma. Throughout the pendency of the case, Jones repeatedly lied to law enforcement and the grand jury about witnessing defendant Matthews’ assaulting her child or being in the Dunkin Donuts on October 13, 2022, in an attempt to hinder the investigation. Jones also deleted messages between her and Matthews from her phone in an attempt to protect Matthews. Joining the announcement was Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department. This case was investigated by the Special Victims Unit of the Homicide Section at the Metropolitan Police Department and was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Emma McArthur and Shauna Payyappilly. 2023 CF2 000873 Contact USADC.Media@usdoj.gov Updated October 16, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Component USAO - District of Columbia

Waipahu Women Sentenced to Two Years in Prison for Pandemic and Tax Fraud While Earning Millions from an Unlicensed Construction Business
Press Release Waipahu Women Sentenced to Two Years in Prison for Pandemic and Tax Fraud While Earning Millions from an Unlicensed Construction Business Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Hawaii HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Heidi Cafirma, 46, of Waipahu, Hawaii, was sentenced on September 30, 2026, by United States District Judge Shanlyn A.S. Park to 24 months in prison followed by 3 years of supervised release for filing false tax returns and wire fraud.  Cafirma was also ordered to forfeit $70,500 and pay up to over $1 million in restitution, which total amount will be determined by the court at a later date.  Cafirma pled guilty pursuant to a plea agreement in December 2025. In 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act created the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (PUA) unemployment insurance program to provide emergency unemployment payments to certain workers whose livelihoods were impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic but who were ineligible for traditional state unemployment insurance benefits, such as business owners, self-employed workers, independent contractors, and those with a limited work history who were out of business or had significantly reduced their services as a direct result of the pandemic.  To obtain either traditional unemployment insurance (UI) or PUA UI benefit payments, claimants could submit a claim online.  If approved, the U.S. Treasury typically deposited payments every week into a claimant’s bank account.  To continue to receive benefit payments, claimants were required to certify on a weekly basis under penalty of law that they remained unemployed or partially employed, and eligible to receive benefit payments. According to court documents, Cafirma admitted that between June 2020 and September 2021, she submitted 22 false claims online for UI benefit payments for herself by repeatedly falsely certifying under penalty of law that she was unemployed and not receiving income, despite knowing that her certifications were false because she received over $1 million in income during that period from her and her husband’s unlicensed construction business.  Cafirma fraudulently obtained at least $70,500 in unemployment insurance and PUA UI benefits to which she was not entitled. Between 2016 and 2020, Cafirma also willfully failed to pay federal and state taxes on over $3.4 million in income from her and her husband’s construction business.  She provided false documents to her tax return preparer that omitted income and then filed false tax returns with the IRS.  Over at least four years, Cafirma took steps to conceal her income by directing construction customers to write checks to her personally rather than to her business, funneling incom

title: Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud
text:
Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud
Press Release Massachusetts Man Charged for His Role in Marriage and Immigration Document Fraud Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Ohio CLEVELAND – A 31-year-old man has been charged for his role in a conspiracy where he allegedly agreed to be paid to enter into a sham marriage to allow a co-conspirator to illegally obtain a green card. A federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Jingming Chen, 31, of Quincy, Massachusetts, with Conspiracy to Commit Marriage Fraud and Immigration Document Fraud. According to allegations in the indictment, Chen, a U.S. citizen, was paid by a Chinese national co-conspirator residing in Aurora, Ohio, to enter into a sham marriage and commit immigration document fraud by fabricating evidence to support the false claim that their marriage was legitimate. They submitted false statements to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS) to obtain lawful permanent resident status—commonly known as a Green Card—and other immigration benefits for the co-conspirator. To carry out the conspiracy, Chen allegedly agreed to receive partial payment at each step of the green card process as they were completed. Chen and the co-conspirator discussed creating a false backstory of their online romance and long-distance relationship, including how they met and who introduced them. They also went so far as to discuss obtaining a prenuptial agreement and opening various joint accounts for banking, cellphone service, insurance, and a discount store membership card. Eventually, the two filed an intent to get married in Quincy, Massachusetts, and Chen directed the co-conspirator to buy a cheap, fake diamond ring to use for the wedding ceremony.  After they married, Chen directed a preparer to submit his USCIS Form I-130, “Petition for Alien Relative,” to document his relationship with a foreign national which would pave the way for the co-conspirator to obtain a green card. The Homeland Security Investigations Cleveland office and the USCIS-Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate in Boston conducted the investigation preceding the indictment. Assistant United States Attorney Brian M. McDonough is leading the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio. If convicted, the defendant faces up to five years in prison. The court will determine the sentence after reviewing the factors unique to this case, including the defendant’s prior criminal record, if any, the defendant’s role in the offenses, and the characteristics of the violations. text:
Connecticut Physician and His Practices Pay More Than $860K to Settle False Claims Act Allegations
Press Release Connecticut Physician and His Practices Pay More Than $860K to Settle False Claims Act Allegations Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Connecticut STEVEN MURPHY, M.D. and his practices, MURPHY MEDICAL ASSOCIATES, LLC and DIAGNOSTIC AND MEDICAL SPECIALISTS OF GREENWICH, LLC, located in Stamford, have entered into a civil settlement agreement with the federal and state governments in which they will pay $866,539 to settle allegations of COVID-19 related fraud and health care fraud.  As part of the settlement, Murphy and his practices agreed to be excluded from all federal health care programs for a period of three years. The government alleges that Murphy and his practices submitted false and fraudulent claims to the Health Resources Services Administration (HRSA), which is a sub-agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, to reimburse Murphy for “uninsured” patients treated during the COVID-19 pandemic.  The government also alleges that Murphy submitted false claims to Medicaid and Medicare for blood testing “panels” allegedly performed by Murphy’s in-house lab. COVID-19 Uninsured Program Fraud In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress passed a series of bills to provide funds to health care providers for COVID-19 testing and treatment for uninsured individuals (the “Uninsured Program”).  The Uninsured Program reimbursed eligible health care providers for COVID-19 testing, treatment, and vaccine administration provided to uninsured individuals.  HRSA was selected to provide oversight and management of the Uninsured Program. An uninsured individual was defined as someone who was “not enrolled” in a government or private health insurance program as of the date of service in question.  Prior to seeking reimbursement from the Uninsured Program, health care providers were required to attest to the government that they had confirmed that the patients for whom they were seeking reimbursement were uninsured. Murphy and his practices participated in the Uninsured Program, attested that the patients for whom they sought payment were uninsured, and received reimbursement from the Uninsured Program for those patients.  The government alleges that Murphy and his practices had information, including copies of insurance cards and other documents, in their files indicating that certain patients for which they made attestations and submitted claims for reimbursement to the Uninsured Program were, in fact, enrolled in government or private health insurance programs.  In addition, Murphy and his practices changed the patient’s insurance identifying information to “Covid19 HRSA Uninsured” in their internal electronic medical records system and then submitted claims and received reimbursement from the Uninsured Program for those patients. On Oct. 14, David Berry Garmarnik, 48, of Tucson, was sentenced by U.S. District Court Judge Rosemary Marquez to 20 years in prison. Garmarnik previously pleaded guilty to one count of Attempted Production of Child Pornography. “Live‑streamed child sexual abuse is one of the most urgent and devastating forms of exploitation, and offenders who fuel it will be met with swift, aggressive, and unrelenting prosecution,” said U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine. “These crimes inflict real‑time harm on real children, and our office will pursue anyone who participates in this abuse, no matter where they hide or how they operate. We are grateful to HSI for its relentless work in dismantling international trafficking networks and for ensuring that those who prey on children are brought to justice.” “This case demonstrates the devastating reality of child exploitation, and the lengths offenders will go to abuse children and conceal their crimes. HSI is committed to identifying these offenders, dismantling the networks that enable their abuse, and working with our domestic and international law enforcement partners to ensure they are held accountable. Protecting children and pursuing those who exploit them remains a priority for HSI, wherever these crimes lead us,” said Jason Stevens, Special Agent in Charge of HSI Phoenix. According to the plea agreement, Garmarnik admitted that he requested and directed sexually explicit conduct of children under the age of 12 and in some cases as young as 7. Additional court records show that HSI identified David Berry Garmarnik as a participant in an international child‑exploitation network that live‑streamed the sexual abuse of minors for paying offenders around the world. Investigators linked Garmarnik to more than 100 online interactions with known or suspected traffickers between 2017 and 2022. Records obtained from Microsoft showed thousands of messages, media files, and call logs consistent with child‑exploitation activity. In addition, financial subpoenas revealed that Garmarnik sent over 100 payments to individuals in the Philippines with no legitimate connection to him, including a known trafficker whose operation involved the abuse of children as young as two years old. After search warrants were executed, Garmarnik admitted he had paid for approximately 100 live‑streamed shows involving minors. Anthony John Rhodes, 37, of Short Pump, is charged with malicious destruction of property by fire. The charges stem from an incident in which Rhodes set a fire in an Elkton retail store during business hours while customers shopped. Kelly O. title: St. Louis County Man Admits Using Fraudulent Deed Filings to Steal At Least 14 Properties
text:
St. Louis County Man Admits Using Fraudulent Deed Filings to Steal At Least 14 Properties
Press Release St. Louis County Man Admits Using Fraudulent Deed Filings to Steal At Least 14 Properties Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – A man on Thursday admitted conspiring to steal at least 14 properties in St. Louis and St. Louis County by filing fraudulent deeds. James L. Townes Jr., 51, of Berkeley, pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to a conspiracy charge. Townes admitted that beginning as early as Sept. 25, 2018, he began filing fraudulent deeds in St. Louis and St. Louis County on properties that belonged to others. The filings falsely claimed that Townes or his relatives had purchased the properties. Townes and his co-defendant, Charnay Bartlett, used fraudulently obtained notary seals to “authenticate” the forged signatures of the true owners of the properties. Townes and Bartlett transferred at least 14 properties to Townes, his companies or his friends and family, his plea agreement says. Townes admitted that his scheme involved the use of the names of 10 or more individuals and that the intended losses associated with his actions exceeded $1,500,000. The real owners had to expend considerable resources to regain the titles to their properties. Others abandoned their properties because they lacked the financial resources to initiate legal action. At least three of the property owners were deceased at the time when their purported signatures were authenticated by Townes and Bartlett. In some cases, Townes gained access to the properties by forcing entry through locked doors and squatting there. Bartlett, 30, pleaded guilty in April to the same conspiracy charge and is scheduled to be sentenced on December 2. Townes is set to be sentenced on January 21. The charge carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or both prison and a fine. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Office of Inspector General, the Social Security Administration Office of Inspector General, the St. Louis County Police Department and the Hazelwood Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Gwen Carroll is prosecuting the case. Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. title: Twice-Deported Illegal Alien from Mexico Arrested on Federal Complaint Charging Him with Possessing 360 Kilograms of Cocaine
text:
Twice-Deported Illegal Alien from Mexico Arrested on Federal Complaint Charging Him with Possessing 360 Kilograms of Cocaine
Press Release Twice-Deported Illegal Alien from Mexico Arrested on Federal Complaint Charging Him with Possessing 360 Kilograms of Cocaine Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California RIVERSIDE, California – A twice-deported illegal immigrant from Mexico has been arrested on a federal criminal complaint charging him with possessing approximately 360 kilograms (793.7 pounds) of cocaine in his San Bernardino County apartment, the Justice Department announced today. José María Mena Rosales, 38, of Fontana, was arrested on Wednesday and is charged with possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Rosales made his initial appearance on Thursday in United States District Court in Riverside. United States Magistrate Judge David T. Bristow ordered Rosales released on $50,000 bond. No plea was taken. Rosales’s arraignment is scheduled for November 10. According to an affidavit filed with the complaint, in February 2026, law enforcement investigating a Mexico-based drug trafficking organization learned that a large quantity of cocaine was to be delivered in four suitcases to Rosales at a public parking lot in Fontana. Rosales later retrieved the cocaine from the parking lot and drove to his apartment, where he unloaded the suitcases of narcotics into a garage. Law enforcement executed a search warrant at Rosales’s garage and apartment and seized approximately 360 kilograms of cocaine spread across 17 cardboard boxes. The four empty suitcases were found in the garage. Law enforcement officers confirmed Rosales’s identity with his California driver’s license and found several cell phones that contained text messages between Rosales and the individual who arranged the cocaine delivery. According to court documents, Rosales was deported from the United States in May 2014 and June 2014. A criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. If convicted, Mena would face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in federal prison and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison. The FBI is investigating this matter with assistance from the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. Assistant United States Attorney Courtney N. Williams of the Transnational Organized Crime Section is prosecuting this case. title: Two Florida defendants sentenced to prison for nearly $900,000 health care scam
text:
Two Florida defendants sentenced to prison for nearly $900,000 health care scam
Press Release Two Florida defendants sentenced to prison for nearly $900,000 health care scam Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Kansas TOPEKA, KAN. – Two defendants received prison sentences following an $897,405 health care scheme where they used their pharmaceutical service to bill Medicare for thousands of unnecessary and illegal prescriptions. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. According to court documents, the following defendants pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, mail fraud, and wire fraud: Steven Anthony Churchill, 39, of Boca Raton, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison; Samson Kollelil Solomon, 28, of Pompano Beach, Florida, was sentenced to 24 months in prison; and Fawn Lickteig, 46, of Lawrence, Kansas, will be sentenced on November 10, 2026. In March 2020, Steven Churchill bought Free State Pharmacy (FSP) in Lawrence, Kansas, but under the name of a now deceased, accused coconspirator. FSP operated as a mail-order pharmacy despite representing itself to Medicare as a retail pharmacy. FSP contracted with Fawn Lickteig’s company, Pharmacy Consulting, to complete and submit its applications to Medicare and other health care related government entities. As part of the scheme, FSP acquired information from telemedicine companies, including names and addresses of patients. FSP employees then filled and shipped medications to these people even though the doctors who wrote the prescriptions had not physically examined or conducted proper telemedicine visits with the patients. FSP received calls from patients unexpectedly receiving medical products, and some patients returned the products to FSP. FSP prioritized the filling of prescriptions based on the amount of profit Medicare would ultimately pay the pharmacy. The majority of the medications prescribed were high-dollar dermatological products. Although FSP was based in Kansas, most of the beneficiaries were Floridians, with 948 claims for Florida residents and 381 claims for Kansas residents. Of the 40 prescribing physicians who worked with FSP, 15 were under investigation at the time for referring medically unnecessary services. title: Lincoln Man Sentenced for Conspiracy to Distribute Methamphetamine
text:
Lincoln Man Sentenced for Conspiracy to Distribute Methamphetamine
Press Release Lincoln Man Sentenced for Conspiracy to Distribute Methamphetamine Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nebraska United States Attorney Lesley A. Woods announced that Jessie Feaster, Jr., 50, of Lincoln, Nebraska, was sentenced on October 15, 2026, in federal court in Lincoln for conspiracy to distribute/possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of methamphetamine mixture and 50 grams or more of methamphetamine actual. United States District Judge Susan M. Bazis sentenced Feaster to 130 months’ imprisonment. There is no parole in the federal system. After Feaster’s release from prison, he will begin a 5-year term of supervised release. On October 10, 2025, investigators with the Lincoln Lancaster County Narcotics Task Force were conducting surveillance on co-defendant David Leibbrandt’s Lincoln residence.  They saw a U.S. Postal Service truck arrive and the driver left a package on the porch.  A short time later, someone came out of the house and retrieved the package.  About an hour later, Feaster, Jr. (“Feaster”) arrived at Leibbrandt’s residence and went inside.  After a few minutes, Feaster returned to his vehicle and left. Investigators followed Feaster to another location in Lincoln where Feaster was contacted and he agreed to let them search his car.  A sandwich bag was found on the front passenger seat which contained approximately one pound of methamphetamine.  Purity testing at the Nebraska State Patrol Crime Lab showed at least 410 grams of actual (pure) methamphetamine. Later the same day, investigators executed a search warrant at Leibbrandt’s residence.  During that search, they found seven bags containing methamphetamine with a total weight of more than 2.7 kilograms.  Purity testing on one of the packages showed at least 1.8 kilograms of actual methamphetamine.  Leibbrandt was arrested and agreed to talk to investigators.  He admitted receiving 10 pounds of methamphetamine earlier that day and said he had already sold more than three pounds from that quantity, including the pound he sold to Feaster. Leibbrandt pleaded guilty to the same conspiracy charge and was sentenced on September 24, 2026, to 135 months’ imprisonment and a 5-year term of supervised release. This case was investigated by the Lincoln/Lancaster County Narcotics Task Force. Contact Amy Donato 402-661-3700 Updated October 16, 2026 Component USAO - Nebraska

Northern Nevada Man Indicted for Federal Child Sexual Abuse Material Crimes
Press Release Northern Nevada Man Indicted for Federal Child Sexual Abuse Material Crimes Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada RENO – A Reno resident has been arrested and made his initial appearance in federal court yesterday for allegedly distributing and possessing child sexual abuse material (CSAM). “There is absolutely no room for leniency when it comes to the exploitation of children,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “Our office, alongside our law enforcement partners, will use every aggressive legal avenue available to dismantle this destructive cycle and ensure that predators face the maximum severity of federal law.” “Not only did Mr. Stockinger exploit these children, he further victimized them by distributing vile images of their abuse to other predators,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Field Office. “His arrest marks the first step toward ensuring he is held fully accountable for these horrific crimes. The FBI will continue to deploy every available resource through our Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Task Force to investigate, pursue, and bring to justice the dangerous predators who target our most vulnerable.” According to allegations in the indictment, beginning about June 5, 2026, to about June 30, 2026, Zachary Steven Stockinger distributed and possessed child sexual abuse material of children younger than 12 years old engaged in sexually explicit conduct. Stockinger is charged with one count of distribution of child pornography and one count of possession of child pornography. A trial has been scheduled for December 15, 2026, before United States District Judge Miranda M. Du. If convicted, Stockinger faces a minimum penalty of five years in prison and a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison. This case was investigated by the FBI. Assistant United States Attorney Afroza Yeasmin is prosecuting the case. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. title: Baltimore Felon Pleads Guilty to Firearm Charges
text:
Baltimore Felon Pleads Guilty to Firearm Charges
Press Release Baltimore Felon Pleads Guilty to Firearm Charges Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maryland Baltimore, Maryland – A Baltimore man pled guilty in federal court to firearm-possession charges. Arsenio Hall, 37, is charged with possession of a firearm and ammunition by a prohibited person. Hall is prohibited from possessing firearms and ammunition due to a prior felony conviction.  Those convictions include two for second-degree assault, including a domestically related assault, along with drug-related convictions. Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Special Agent in Charge Charles Doerrer, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF), and Commissioner Richard Worley, Baltimore Police Department (BPD). According to court documents, on December 19, 2024, members of BPD’s SWAT Team arrived at Hall’s residence to assist Baltimore County Police Department detectives with executing an arrest warrant on Hall and a search-and-seizure warrant on his residence. These warrants were related to a November 2024 shooting in Baltimore County. During the search, officers recovered a semi-automatic rifle from a baby crib inside of Hall’s bedroom. Hall faces a maximum of 15 years in prison for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person.  U.S. District Court Judge Ellen L. Hollander set sentencing for Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027, at 11 a.m. Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. This prosecution is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) and Project Safe Home. These programs bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce violent crime and gun violence, and to make our neighborhoods safer for everyone. On May 26, 2021, the Department launched a violent crime reduction strategy strengthening PSN based on these core principles: fostering trust and legitimacy in our communities, supporting community-based organizations that help prevent violence from occurring in the first place, setting focused and strategic enforcement priorities, and measuring the results. Project Safe Home is an initiative under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) through the Office on Violence Against Women (OVW) to reduce domestic violence and prevent escalation to lethal violence by targeting offenders who use or possess handguns with a history of Domestic Violence. title: Brazilian Man Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Managerial Role in Conspiracy to Launder Tens of Millions of Dollars in Illicit Cash Proceeds
text:
Brazilian Man Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Managerial Role in Conspiracy to Launder Tens of Millions of Dollars in Illicit Cash Proceeds
Press Release Brazilian Man Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Managerial Role in Conspiracy to Launder Tens of Millions of Dollars in Illicit Cash Proceeds Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Sixth Defendant Sentenced in $30 Million Multi-State Laundering Scheme Ygor Fokin Saviolli, 35, a Brazilian national, was sentenced today to 12 years in prison for his role as a manager and supervisor in a money laundering organization that laundered more than $30 million in illicit proceeds, including the proceeds of drug trafficking. On September 24, five co-defendants received sentences ranging from 94 months in prison to 12 months and one day in prison. Gabriel Cezar Menezes, 29, a Brazilian national, was sentenced to 94 months; Omar Aliperti De Mello Correa, 34, a U.S. citizen, was sentenced to 30 months; Leandro De Avila Goncalves, 43, a Brazilian national, was sentenced to 24 months; and Joao Andrade De Mello, 29, and Tadeu Sebastiane Rabelo Alves Barbosa, 30, both Brazilian nationals, were each sentenced to 12 months and one day. The Brazilian national defendants were illegally residing in the United States at the time of their arrests. According to court documents, Saviolli, Menezes, Correa, Goncalves, De Mello, and Barbosa were part of a sophisticated money laundering organization that operated across the United States and spanned several countries. Members of the conspiracy arranged for U.S.-based couriers to receive bulk cash proceeds from the sale of controlled substances and then to deposit the cash at banks across the country in order to conceal and return those profits to, among others, the sources of drug supply operating outside the United States. Dozens of pickups across the country were coordinated through WhatsApp message chains that included facilitators and couriers. Saviolli provided upfront funds to facilitate the operations of the money laundering organization and oversaw the receipt and laundering of the bulk cash drug proceeds. Menezes also served as a facilitator, providing direction to and oversight of couriers, and personally picked up bulk cash on multiple occasions. Correa, De Mello, Barbosa, and Goncalves all served as couriers for the money laundering organization, conducting bulk cash pickups in cities including Atlanta, Charlotte, Chicago, Cleveland, Minneapolis, Rochester, and Tampa, among others. Over the course of the conspiracy, the organization concealed more than $30 million in cash. In June 2026, the defendants’ guilty pleas to conspiracy to commit money laundering were accepted by the district court. Assistant Attorney General A. title: Federal Detainees to Be Relocated to Detention Facilities in Mecklenburg County; Partnership Between the U.S. Attorney’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office Brings Federal Resources to North Carolina
text:
Federal Detainees to Be Relocated to Detention Facilities in Mecklenburg County; Partnership Between the U.S. Attorney’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office Brings Federal Resources to North Carolina
Press Release Federal Detainees to Be Relocated to Detention Facilities in Mecklenburg County; Partnership Between the U.S. Attorney’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office Brings Federal Resources to North Carolina Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of North Carolina CHARLOTTE, N.C. – U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson, U.S. Marshal Terry Burgin, and Mecklenburg County Sheriff Garry McFadden today announced a new agreement between the Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) and the U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) to relocate federal detainees from detention facilities outside of North Carolina to facilities in Mecklenburg County. “Housing federal detainees in Mecklenburg County whose cases are pending in this district not only brings millions of federal dollars to North Carolina that otherwise went to other states, it benefits the federal justice system. It means defendants are closer to their attorneys—making it easier to prepare their defense and thus move cases faster—and closer to their families, which makes rehabilitation and reentry to society more likely to be successful. It also means shorter, quicker, and cheaper transportation to court, which makes it easier to schedule hearings and trials,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson. “I am so thankful to Sheriff Garry McFadden and Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge for making this partnership possible.” “The U.S. Marshals Service is excited to once again house federal detainees with the Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office. The MCSO and the USMS have a long-standing partnership. The reopening of Mecklenburg County Detention Center North will allow for the continued due process of federal detainees and ensure the federal judicial system operates efficiently,” said Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge. “When law enforcement and criminal justice agencies work together through transparent collaboration, open communication, and an unwavering commitment to public safety, we reinforce accountability and the integrity of the justice system while demonstrating the unity and professionalism our communities expect and deserve. Today stands as a clear example of that commitment by bringing federal detainees back to the Sheriff’s Office’s North facility. I commend U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson and Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Chris Edge for their leadership and partnership in supporting the Sheriff’s Office throughout this process,” said Sheriff Garry McFadden. text:
Floridian sentenced to federal prison, ordered to pay $2.8M in restitution for money laundering scheme in the Eastern District of Texas
Press Release Floridian sentenced to federal prison, ordered to pay $2.8M in restitution for money laundering scheme in the Eastern District of Texas Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Texas PLANO, Texas – A Palm Bay, Florida man has been sentenced to federal prison for a money laundering scheme in the Eastern District of Texas, announced U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs. Joshua Thomas Jackson, 41, pleaded guilty to money laundering and was sentenced to 51 months in federal prison by U.S. District Judge Sean D. Jordan on October 15, 2026. According to information presented in court, Jackson engaged in a scheme to defraud individuals using false representations and statements.  To facilitate the scheme, Jackson created business entities and marketed opportunities to invest in real estate development, purchases, and rehabilitation schemes. As Jackson carried out his scheme, he falsely represented that funds investors provided would be used to purchase real property or distressed residential properties, that the investors funds were secure and would be repaid within a defined period of time, and that his business activities and the victims’ investments were secure and profitable. During the period of his scheme Jackson received over $3 million from investors and caused losses to investors exceeding $2.8 million. “Investor fraud is a destructive crime and causes significant losses across our nation,” said U.S. Attorney Jay R. Combs. “Together, with our partners at the FBI, we will continue to investigate and prosecute this type of fraud in the Eastern District of Texas, bring justice to these perpetrators, and seek restitution for victims.” This case was investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys in the Plano office. ### Updated October 16, 2026 Topics Fraud Financial Fraud Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Texas, Eastern

title: Leader of Lubbock Bandidos Motorcycle Club sentenced to federal prison for meth distribution
text:
Leader of Lubbock Bandidos Motorcycle Club sentenced to federal prison for meth distribution
Press Release Leader of Lubbock Bandidos Motorcycle Club sentenced to federal prison for meth distribution Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Texas LUBBOCK, Texas – United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould today announced that a Lubbock man who led a high-purity methamphetamine trafficking operation was sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison. Steven Glenn Ryals, 72, also known as “Hot Tub,” was convicted of possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine. U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix imposed the 135-month sentence today. “Steven Ryals exploited his leadership of the Bandidos’ Lubbock chapter to push high purity methamphetamine into our community,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “Today’s sentence sends a clear message: we will aggressively pursue those who traffic dangerous drugs and dismantle the drug distribution networks that threaten West Texans.” “Today’s sentence reflects the FBI’s continued commitment to protecting our communities from the dangers of high purity narcotics and the criminal networks that distribute them,” said FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock. “This case underscores the impact of strong partnerships among federal, state, and local agencies and our shared resolve to disrupt drug trafficking organizations and hold traffickers accountable.” According to court documents, Ryals was the President of the Bandidos Motorcycle Club’s Lubbock Notorious Chapter and had served with the club for over 50 years. Federal law enforcement began investigating Ryals and other members in early 2025 for distributing methamphetamine in the Lubbock area. On Feb. 27, FBI agents and the Lubbock Anti-Gang Center executed a search warrant at the Bandidos clubhouse, which also served as Ryals’s residence. During that search, agents discovered approximately 3.2 pounds of suspected methamphetamine inside a locked filing‑cabinet drawer, along with Bandidos paraphernalia and tools used to package and distribute narcotics. At sentencing, prosecutors outlined the results of DEA laboratory testing confirming the substance was 1,449.6 grams of methamphetamine hydrochloride at 98% purity, an amount consistent only with high‑level distribution. Additional methamphetamine was found in Ryals’s bedroom closet and in his vehicle during a traffic stop on the same day, all of which he admitted possessing with intent to distribute. Ryals was previously convicted of methamphetamine trafficking and in 1999 received an identical 135‑month sentence for that offense. The FBI, the Lubbock Texas Anti‑Gang (TAG) Center and the Caprock High‑Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) conducted the investigation. title: Convicted Drug Dealer Charged with Trafficking Methamphetamine While Armed with Firearm, Extended Magazine, and Drum Magazine
text:
Convicted Drug Dealer Charged with Trafficking Methamphetamine While Armed with Firearm, Extended Magazine, and Drum Magazine
Press Release Convicted Drug Dealer Charged with Trafficking Methamphetamine While Armed with Firearm, Extended Magazine, and Drum Magazine Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Hawaii HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Shalom Tuimalealiifano, 44, of Honolulu, Hawaii, was indicted on October 15, 2026 with possessing with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking, and unlawful possession of ammunition as a convicted felon. According to court records, Tuimalealiifano possessed methamphetamine with the intent to distribute it to others, as well as a loaded pistol with a 31-round extended magazine, which he used in furtherance of his drug trafficking.  Tuimalealiifano, who has a prior felony conviction for drug trafficking, was also charged with unlawfully possessing ammunition, including 39 rounds in a separate drum magazine. If convicted, Tuimalealiifano faces at least 20 years and up to life in prison, a fine of up to $20,000,000, plus a term of supervised release. The charges in the indictment are merely accusations, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.  In the case of conviction, any sentence would be imposed by a United States District Judge based on the statutory sentencing factors and the advisory United States Sentencing Guidelines. The FBI is investigating the case. Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Heidi Turner is prosecuting the case. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe.  Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges.  As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe.  PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies.  These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Force, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. title: Final Defendant Sentenced in a Conspiracy to Distribute Counterfeit Pills Containing Fentanyl
text:
Final Defendant Sentenced in a Conspiracy to Distribute Counterfeit Pills Containing Fentanyl
Press Release Final Defendant Sentenced in a Conspiracy to Distribute Counterfeit Pills Containing Fentanyl Friday, October 16, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Kentucky LEXINGTON, Ky. – A Lexington, Ky., man, Quentin Montez Leavell, 33, was sentenced to 144 months of imprisonment yesterday by U.S. District Judge Chad Meredith for conspiracy to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl, distribution of fentanyl, and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime. According to his plea agreement, from February 2021 to July 2021, Leavell agreed with others, including codefendants, Dominque Cornell Duff and Lakwon Marquis Givens, to distribute fentanyl contained in counterfeit pills that resembled Percocet, with markings of “M, 30.” Leavell further admitted that he possessed a firearm to protect himself and to deter others from attempting to rob or steal drugs and/or money from him. Codefendants Duff and Givens were sentenced in September 2026, to 155 months and 170 months, respectively, for their roles in the conspiracy. Jason Parman, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Kentucky, Dennis M. Fetting, Special Agent in Charge, Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and Chief Lawrence Weathers, Lexington Police Department, jointly announced the sentences. The investigation was conducted by the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Lexington Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Bradbury prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States. This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. – END – Contact CONTACT: Jenny Parker PHONE: (859) 685-4906 E-MAIL: jenny.parker@usdoj.gov Updated October 16, 2026 Topics Homeland Security Task Force Drug Trafficking Opioids Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Kentucky, Eastern

Members discussed the response to the public consultation, which received nearly 500,000 responses via an online survey, post, emails and phone calls. title: September 28, 2026 - FDA Approves First Treatment for MCT8 Deficiency
text:
September 28, 2026 - FDA Approves First Treatment for MCT8 Deficiency
FDA News Release FDA Approves First Treatment for MCT8 Deficiency First therapy to bypass the broken transporter at the root of this very rare genetic disease and to decrease elevated blood thyroid hormone levels For Immediate Release: September 28, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Emcitate (tiratricol) tablets for oral suspension to treat peripheral thyrotoxicosis (excess thyroid hormone levels in the blood that causes symptoms, such as rapid heart rate, increased blood pressure and adverse effects on metabolism) in patients with MCT8 deficiency, also known as Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome. Emcitate is the first therapy approved by the FDA to treat symptoms of this very rare, devastating genetic disease. This approval reflects the FDA’s dedication to patients with rare genetic diseases, many of whom have serious unmet medical needs. “Until now, patients living with MCT8 deficiency and their families had no FDA-approved treatment option,” said Marina Zemskova, M.D., Deputy Director of the Division of General Endocrinology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Emcitate’s approval reflects the FDA’s deep commitment to patients with rare conditions who are in need of meaningful treatment options.” MCT8 deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that primarily affects males. The condition is caused by a faulty gene that provides instructions for making the MCT8 transporter, a critical protein responsible for carrying thyroid hormone into the brain. Because thyroid hormone cannot cross the blood-brain barrier without the MCT8 transporter, the brain receives too little of this hormone, while excessive levels of the hormone build up in the bloodstream. Many patients with MCT8 deficiency experience a range of debilitating effects, including the inability to walk or sit independently, absent or severely limited speech, intellectual disability, feeding difficulties and chronic stress on the heart and metabolism. “The challenge in treating MCT8 deficiency has always been that the protein needed to deliver thyroid hormone into cells is the one that isn’t working,” said Hylton V. Joffe, M.D., MMSc, Director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This drug sidesteps that problem, as its active ingredient, tiratricol, can enter cells on its own without relying on the broken transporter, leading to a decrease in the elevated blood thyroid hormone levels.” The effectiveness of Emcitate was evaluated in two clinical studies in patients ranging in age from infants to adults, including an international, multi-center, randomized, placebo-controlled trial ( NCT05579327 ) and a longer-term open-label study. text:
Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
October 15, 2026 Research Product Bringing GPT‑Rosalind to academic research labs Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery. Apply for access (opens in a new window) Loading… Share We’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind ⁠ , our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench ⁠ (opens in a new window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval. Academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn. Accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this plan, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research. Supporting the research behind future breakthroughs Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research. The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology. Curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a new generation of vaccines and therapies. Academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab. How academic labs are using GPT‑Rosalind OpenAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. title: Bringing the magic: Google breaks open a bottleneck in quantum computing
text:
Bringing the magic: Google breaks open a bottleneck in quantum computing
Bringing the magic: Google breaks open a bottleneck in quantum computing Oct 15, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We've shown that magic state cultivation works on Google Quantum AI hardware. Emma Rosenfeld Research Scientist, Google Quantum AI Craig Gidney Quantum Software Engineer, Google Quantum AI Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Google Quantum AI has demonstratively opened up a key bottleneck in quantum computing: we’ve shown that “magic state cultivation” works in practice on our Willow processor, reducing errors about 40x compared to without it. This breakthrough, published today in Science , is a crucial step towards scaling up quantum computing to practical use. The "magic state" bottleneck Since 2004, long before quantum computing was a practical engineering pursuit, researchers have foreseen a particularly tricky bottleneck. To achieve “universal” quantum computing and execute useful programs, you need to be able to run (and error-correct ) a specific set of quantum operations. You can do this by first creating what are called "magic states," so dubbed because they can help you create the operations you need for going beyond classical computing. But there’s a catch: creating high-quality, error-corrected magic states is incredibly resource-heavy. Some estimates have shown that up to 95% of a quantum computer’s entire capacity might need to be dedicated to making them — leaving little room for actual computing. An extra challenge is that once you use a magic state, you can’t re-use it, making magic states a scarce resource. So for 20 years, researchers have been chipping away at this cost of magic, bringing it lower and lower. How we made this breakthrough In 2024, Google Quantum AI researchers Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones harnessed an idea from the literature, refined it, and developed what we now call “magic state cultivation.” Their approach promised an especially large reduction. The idea was that cultivation would act like a filter. You would inject a noisy state into a small region on a quantum chip, and then run a series of highly coordinated measurements to check for errors and remove any flawed attempts. Craig and team showed how that would let you grow, or “cultivate,” an exceptionally pure, low-error quantum state that you could simultaneously adapt into a larger, useful encoding. On paper, it looked great. If we could make this idea actually work on our quantum hardware, it could substantially reduce the size of the quantum computer needed for practical tasks. In practice — and on par with developing many new technologies — it required a whole series of technical innovations and engineering. Be There for the Beginning: Celebrate the Launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark Explore a new era of local AI, join launch celebrations around the world and #ShareYourSpark. October 15, 2026 by Shreevar Rastogi 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! A new beginning for Windows PCs starts tomorrow with the launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark — one PC built for creators, gamers and AI agents. All are invited to celebrate with NVIDIA and partners at launch events around the world. Share Your Spark Every PC has a story. What was your first Windows PC, and what did it spark a love for? title: How we're helping the world prepare for natural disasters
text:
How we're helping the world prepare for natural disasters
How we're helping the world prepare for natural disasters Oct 15, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Our north star is simple yet ambitious: No one should be surprised by a natural disaster. Yossi Matias VP, Google & GM, Google Research Kate Brandt Chief Sustainability Officer Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today is International ShakeOut Day , when millions practice earthquake drills. Our Android Earthquake Alerts System turns smartphones into a global network that can warn people before shaking arrives, and it's expanding to more countries and regions. When a natural disaster strikes, early warnings and trusted information help people prepare, respond, and stay safe. Earthquakes are only one part of our crisis resilience efforts at Google. Our AI models also help people prepare for other natural disasters: Floods: Our flood forecasting technology provides up to seven days' notice for riverine floods for more than two billion people in 150 countries and up to 24 hours' notice for urban flash floods . Cyclones: WeatherNext can predict cyclones up to 15 days out. Wildfires: Near-real-time fire boundary maps are live in 34 countries, and FireSat , a global satellite constellation, is designed to detect and track fires as small as a classroom within 20 minutes once completed. In 2025 alone, Google helped connect people with crisis information more than 10 million times per day, on average. Our north star is simple yet ambitious: No one should be surprised by a natural disaster. Learn more about our progress on crisis resilience and how we are working with partners and communities around the world to better prepare for natural disasters in our new Crisis Resilience white paper . Posted in:

title: Android earthquake alerts now available in more than 200 regions
text:
Android earthquake alerts now available in more than 200 regions
Android earthquake alerts now available in more than 200 regions Oct 15, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We’ve sent over one billion Android earthquake alerts. Now, we’re expanding alerts to more places and adding new details, helping more people take action and stay safe. Boone Spooner Group Product Manager, Earthquake Alerts Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link A few seconds of warning when an earthquake hits can give you crucial time to take cover and protect yourself and your loved ones. To make these early warnings possible at scale, we built the Android Earthquake Alerts System — the world’s largest mobile-based earthquake detection network. Since launching in 2021, we’ve sent over one billion alerts to help people stay safe before the shaking even starts. Today, we’re expanding the system from 98 countries and regions to more than 200 — including Panama, Guatemala and many more. We’re also improving our latest “Be Ready” alert to give you more information in seconds. If an earthquake occurs in a region where alerts are active, Android users can expect to see one of three alerts: Be Aware: A straightforward alert for estimated light shaking, letting you know an earthquake has been detected nearby. Be Ready: A detailed alert for stronger shaking, alerting you to prepare to take action. Take Action: A full-screen alert for moderate to heavy shaking, giving you immediate advice on how to stay safe. We’ve built-out our Be Ready alert with new helpful guidance. In the coming months, you’ll see a map with a radius of where we’ve detected shaking, estimated earthquake magnitude, action you can take, and a button to learn more about the earthquake as information comes in. Updated "Be Ready" alert coming soon Our physical safety products are deeply important to us. While we hope they never get used, we’re grateful to be able to bring more information to more people when they need it most. Learn more about the Android Earthquake Alerts System and where it is active . 1 To see how we're helping communities around the world better prepare for earthquakes and other natural disasters, read our new Crisis Resilience white paper . To help meet this moment, we’re evolving our partnerships as newsrooms adapt to these shifts in user preferences and new technology. Since launching our News AI pilot program last year with a range of news partners, like The Washington Examiner and The Washington Post, more than 400 publications worldwide are now participating in this program. Our newest partners range from global outlets like Axios, CNN, The Financial Times, and Forbes, to local publishers like Post and Courier, Texas Tribune, Oil City News, and Shaw Media in the U.S. Through this licensing program, we pay participating news publications for the delivery and use of enhanced content to develop new AI features. For example, these experiences include in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages offering people helpful context before they click and customizable audio briefings for listeners. With clear attribution and direct links, these features build meaningful new ways for readers to connect with the sources they value.
